finding: PhiUSIIL's URLSimilarityIndex is not merely a strong predictor - it is a label artifact. The feature is CONSTANT on the legitimate class.

single_rule_performance.comment: Every single error is a phishing row that happens to take the legitimate-class constant. There are no legitimate rows below 100 at all.

reproduce: from src.preprocessing import get_xy; X,y = get_xy('phiusiil'); u = X['URLSimilarityIndex']; assert (u[y==0] == 100).all(); ((u < 100).astype(int) == y).mean()
why_this_matters: The reported ~99-100% accuracy on PhiUSIIL measures the presence of this artifact, not phishing detection. E1 returns accuracy 0.99999 +/- 0.00001 for all four models, and all three tuned learners converge to an identical CV F1 of 0.9999857 - the signature of a saturated, trivially separable target.
SHAP rankings on PhiUSIIL are anchored by this feature: URLSimilarityIndex is the top-ranked feature in every half, every seed, and at every convergence sample size.

This inflates the E2 within-dataset consistency baseline. PhiUSIIL's tau of 0.9190 is high partly because one deterministic feature pins the top of the ranking in both halves, whereas the UCI dataset (no such feature; best single-feature accuracy 0.8736) yields tau 0.7683. The within-dataset ceiling is therefore dataset-dependent and cannot be assumed to be a single constant in Phase B.

Any cross-dataset SHAP comparison in Phase B compares a near-deterministic attribution profile against a genuinely contested one. A with/without-URLSimilarityIndex variant is strongly advised so the comparison is not dominated by this artifact.
